title: Theorem A
body_md:
Let Assumption~\ref{ass:M} hold, $0<a_{\min}\le a_{\max}$, $B\ge1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.
There is an explicit operator network $N_\varepsilon$ with $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}$-layers (or with $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{mix}}$-layers) and input channels $(a,f)$, of depth $N=O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q))$, whose parameters depend only on $B$, $a_{\min}$, $a_{\max}$, $\varepsilon$ and $K$---not on $X$, $\mu$, a dimension, or the spectrum of $L_0$ beyond $\lambda_1\ge1$---such that
\[
    \sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal B}(B)}\ \sup_{\norm{f}_{L^2}\le1,\ \int f=0}\ \norm{G(a,f)-N_\varepsilon(a,f)}_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon .
\]
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $\theta\in(0,1]$, $0<a_{\min}\le a_{\max}$, $B\ge1$, and let $\bar a$, $q$ and $\mathcal{A}_\theta$ be as in \eqref{eq:intro-constants} and \eqref{eq:intro-class}.
For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ there is an explicit operator network $N_\varepsilon$ with $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}$-layers (or with $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{mix}}$-layers) and input channels $(a,f)$ such that
\[
    \sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}_\theta}\ \sup_{\norm{f}_{L^2}\le1,\ \int f=0}\ \norm{G(a,f)-N_\varepsilon(a,f)}_{\dot H^1(\mathbb{T}^d)}\le\varepsilon.
\]
Namely, with
\[
    \eta_0:=\min\Bigl\{\frac{\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)^2}{8},\ \frac{1-q}2\Bigr\},
\]
$K^{\mathrm{net}}$ and $R_m$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:step} at $(\theta,B,\eta_0)$, and $b:=a/\bar a-1$,
\[
    v_0=R_mf,\qquad v_{i+1}=R_mf-K^{\mathrm{net}} v_i\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad N_\varepsilon(a,f)=\bar a^{-1}v_N,
\]
\[
    N=\max\Bigl\{0,\Bigl\lceil\frac{\log\frac4{\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)}}{\log(1/q)}\Bigr\rceil\Bigr\}\qquad(N=0\text{ if }q=0).
\]

name: Emulation of the Darcy solution operator on $\TT^d$

label: rem:structure
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:structure}
All constants are independent of $d$ for the class $\mathcal{A}_\theta$ defined through the Wiener norm; if the class is described instead through $H^\sigma(\mathbb{T}^d)$ with $\sigma>1+\theta+d/2$, the dimension enters through $B$ via the embedding constant.
A Wiener ball is an $\ell^1$-type class, much smaller than a Sobolev ball when $d$ is large.
For $\theta=1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:dirichlet-main} (through Corollary~\ref{cor:torus-C2}) dominates Theorem~\ref{thm:main} in every respect: it covers the strictly larger class $\{\norm{\nabla b}_\infty+\norm{\Delta b}_\infty\le B\}$, which contains the Wiener ball $\{\norm{b}_{A^2}\le B/2\}$, with the same scheme, the same depth $N$ and $d$-independent constants, and with a much better recipe---at equal $B$, the band radius is $\sqrt\Lambda=20B/\eta_0$ instead of $60B/\eta_0$, the heat time satisfies $t^{-1/2}=5B/\eta_0$ instead of $\sqrt{40}\cdot20B/\eta_0\approx126B/\eta_0$, so that the resolution scale $K_{\mathrm{req}}$ of Remark~\ref{rem:resolution-intro} is smaller by a factor of about $6$ and the multiplier $1/(2t)$ of the product defect by a factor $640$.
These factors compare the two recipes at the same value of $B$, that is, on different classes; on the same class, the Wiener ball $\{\norm{b}_{A^2}\le B\}$, which lies in the class of Corollary~\ref{cor:torus-C2} with $2B$ in place of $B$, they are about $1.5$ for the band radius, $12.6$ for $t^{-1/2}$, $3.2$ for $K_{\mathrm{req}}$ and $160$ for $1/(2t)$.
The numerical consequence is visible in Table~\ref{tab:numerics}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is therefore the main result only for $\theta<1$, where it covers coefficients with fewer than two derivatives in the Wiener scale, and for the sharpness statement of Remark~\ref{rem:sharpness}.

The construction is linear in $f$, and $N_\varepsilon(a,f)=N_\varepsilon(a,\Pi f)$ because $R_m$ and $I-P_T$ annihilate constants; for fixed $f$ it is a polynomial map of degree $N$ in $a$; and it uses no activation function.
Indeed, $v_N=\sum_{j=0}^N(-K^{\mathrm{net}})^jR_mf$ and $K^{\mathrm{net}}$ is linear in $b=a/\bar a-1$, so the $j$-th term is a $j$-linear form in $b$, and $\bar a$ is a class constant.
The depth $N$ is $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q))$, all blocks share their parameters, and all parameters are functions of $(\theta,B,a_{\min},a_{\max},\varepsilon)$.
The heat family uses $(N+1)(m+3)$ heat applications (Proposition~\ref{prop:counts}); in the mixed family the scheme is determined by the five theorem-prescribed scalars $(s,t,\tau,T,\bar a)$ and the integer $N$, and uses $3N+3$ heat and $N+1$ resolvent applications (Corollary~\ref{cor:mixed}).

name: Structure of the construction

label: rem:resolution-intro
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:resolution-intro}
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} concerns continuum operators, and logarithmic depth and operator-application counts do not imply a cheap discretised realisation.
The proof controls the heat layers up to the frequency
\[
    K_{\mathrm{req}}=\max\{\sqrt\Lambda,t^{-1/2}\}\asymp\Bigl(\frac{B\kappa^2}{\varepsilon\bar a}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}
\]
per direction (Proposition~\ref{prop:counts}(e)); a spectral discretisation on which the proved bounds are guaranteed must resolve these frequencies, which leads to arithmetic cost polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ with exponent $d/\theta$ (Section~\ref{subsec:discretised}).
This requirement is sufficient for the proof and is not shown to be necessary for the scheme; the example of Section~\ref{sec:numerics} works on a far coarser grid.
On the other hand, every band-limited approximation of $\dot H^1$ output from $L^2$ data needs $K\gtrsim1/(\varepsilon\bar a)$ modes per direction.

For $\theta=1$ the two scalings have the same exponent, with a large constant ($K_{\mathrm{req}}\approx253\,(\kappa+1)^2B/(\varepsilon\bar a)$ in the generic case for the recipe of Theorem~\ref{thm:step}, and $K_{\mathrm{req}}=20B/\eta_0=40(\kappa+1)^2B/(\varepsilon\bar a)$ for the recipe of Theorem~\ref{thm:dirichlet-main}), while for $\theta<1$ the exponent $1/\theta$ is larger.
The rate $t^{\theta/2}$ that produces this exponent is attained for the block \eqref{eq:block-intro} over the $A^{1+\theta}$ ball (Remark~\ref{rem:sharpness}), so it cannot be removed by sharper estimates of this block under the present regularity.

label: def:HR
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:HR}
Let $\delta\in(0,1]$ and $\Lambda\in[1,\infty]$.
A function $r\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $r(0)=0$ satisfies \textup{(H$_R$)}{} if
\[
    \abs{\lambda r(\lambda)-1}\le\delta\ \text{ for }\lambda\in[1,\Lambda],
    \qquad
    0\le\lambda r(\lambda)\le1+\delta\ \text{ for }\lambda\in[1,\infty).
\]
For $\Lambda=\infty$ the first condition is required on $[1,\infty)$.
We then write $R_m:=r(L_0)$.

label: lem:HR
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Consequences of \HR

title: Proof
body_md:
On $[1,\Lambda]$, $\abs{r-\lambda^{-1}}=\lambda^{-1}\abs{\lambda r-1}\le\delta\lambda^{-1}$; for $\lambda>\Lambda$, $\lambda r\in[0,1+\delta]$ gives $\abs{\lambda r-1}\le1\le\delta+2$.
The bound on $\abs r$ is immediate.
By the spectral theorem,
\begin{multline*}
    \norm{(R_m-R)g}_1^2=\sum_{k\ne0}\abs{k}^2\abs{r(\abs{k}^2)-\abs{k}^{-2}}^2\abs{\hat g_k}^2\\
    \le\sup_{\lambda\ge1}\lambda^{-1}(\delta+2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\lambda>\Lambda})^2\norm{g}^2
    \le(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})^2\norm{g}^2,
\end{multline*}
and the second estimate in \eqref{eq:HR-consequences} follows in the same way.

label: lem:sinc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sinc}
Let $\delta_0\in(0,1]$ and $\Lambda\ge1$.
Put
\[
    h=\frac{\pi^2}{\pi^2+2\log(1/\delta_0)},\quad
    M=\Bigl\lceil\frac{\log(8\Lambda/\delta_0)}{h}\Bigr\rceil-1,\quad
    N_{\mathrm{sinc}}=\Bigl\lceil\frac{\log\bigl(2\log\frac{8}{h\delta_0}\bigr)}{h}\Bigr\rceil-1,\quad
    T=\log\frac5{\delta_0},
\]
and
\[
    r(\lambda)=\bigl(1-\mathrm{e}^{-T\lambda}\bigr)\,h\sum_{j=-M}^{N_{\mathrm{sinc}}}\mathrm{e}^{jh}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda\mathrm{e}^{jh}}.
\]
Then $r(0)=0$ and $r$ satisfies \textup{(H$_R$)}{} on $[1,\Lambda]$ with $\delta=\delta_0$.
The operator $R_m=r(L_0)=(I-P_T)\,h\sum_{j=-M}^{N_{\mathrm{sinc}}}\mathrm{e}^{jh}P_{\mathrm{e}^{jh}}$ is a composition of $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}$-layers using $m:=M+N_{\mathrm{sinc}}+1$ heat times $\mathrm{e}^{jh}$ and the further time $T$, and
\[
    m=O\Bigl(\log\frac1{\delta_0}\,\log\frac{\Lambda}{\delta_0}\Bigr).
\]

label: lem:product-defect
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:product-defect}
Let $b\in A^0$, $u\in L^2$ and $t>0$.
Then, with $k=k'-\mu$,
\begin{gather*}
    \widehat{\Gamma_t(b,u)}_{k'}=-\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu\,(\mu\cdot k)\,F_t(k,\mu)\,\hat u_k,\\
    F_t(k,\mu)=\mathrm{e}^{-t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)}\varphi(2t\,\mu\cdot k),\qquad
    \varphi(z)=\frac{1-\mathrm{e}^{-z}}{z},\ \varphi(0)=1,
\end{gather*}
and
\[
    0<F_t\le1,\qquad 0\le1-F_t\le\min\bigl\{1,\,2t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)\bigr\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Product defect of a heat layer

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{The multiplier.}
For $b\in A^0$ and $u\in L^2$ the Fourier coefficients of the products are given by absolutely convergent convolutions, and
\[
    \widehat{P_t(bu)}_{k'}=\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu\hat u_k\mathrm{e}^{-t\abs{k+\mu}^2},\qquad
    \widehat{(P_tb\,P_tu)}_{k'}=\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu\mathrm{e}^{-t\abs{\mu}^2}\hat u_k\mathrm{e}^{-t\abs{k}^2}.
\]
Since $\abs{k+\mu}^2=\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2+2\mu\cdot k$, the difference of the $\mu$-terms is
\[
    \hat b_\mu\hat u_k\mathrm{e}^{-t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)}\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{-2t\mu\cdot k}-1\bigr)=-2t(\mu\cdot k)\hat b_\mu\hat u_kF_t(k,\mu);
\]
dividing by $2t$ gives the formula.
$F_t>0$ because $\varphi>0$.

\smallskip
\emph{Upper bound.}
$\abs{\mathrm{e}^{-x}-\mathrm{e}^{-y}}\le\abs{x-y}$ for $x,y\ge0$ gives
\[
    \abs{\mathrm{e}^{-t\abs{k+\mu}^2}-\mathrm{e}^{-t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)}}\le2t\abs{\mu\cdot k},
\]
i.e.\ $F_t\le1$.

\smallskip
\emph{Lower bound.}
Put $A=t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)$ and $z=2t\mu\cdot k$, so that $\abs{z}\le A$.
\emph{Case $z<0$.} Then $\varphi(z)\ge1$ and $F_t\ge\mathrm{e}^{-A}\ge1-A$.
\emph{Case $z\ge0$.} Then $\varphi(z)\ge1-z/2$ (from $\mathrm{e}^{-z}\le1-z+z^2/2$), so
\[
    F_t\ge\mathrm{e}^{-A}(1-z/2)\ge(1-A)(1-A/2)\ge1-\tfrac32A\qquad\text{when }A\le1.
\]
Hence $1-F_t\le2A$ when $A\le1$ (the proof gives $\frac32A$; the factor $2$ is used for round constants later), and $1-F_t<1$ always since $F_t>0$.

label: thm:representation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:representation}
Let $b\in A^1$ be real.
Then, as an identity in $\dot H^1$,
\[
    K_b=\Pi M_b+R\,\Gamma(b,\cdot)-R\,\mathcal{M}_b,
\]
with
\[
    \norm{K_b}_{\mathcal{L}(\dot H^1)}\le\norm{b}_{L^\infty},\qquad
    \norm{R\mathcal{M}_b}_{\mathcal{L}(\dot H^1)}\le2\norm{b}_{A^1}.
\]
If $b\in A^2$, the remainder $K_b-\Pi M_b=R(\Gamma(b,\cdot)-\mathcal{M}_b)$ maps $\dot H^1$ into $\dot H^2$.
head: environment
name: Laplacian-preconditioned operator $=$ multiplication $+$ smoothing

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{The bound on $K_b$.}
It follows from $\abs{\inner{K_bu,v}_{\dot H^1}}=\abs{\int b\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}}\le\norm{b}_\infty\norm{u}_1\norm{v}_1$; it needs only $b\in L^\infty$.

\smallskip
\emph{The identity.}
Let $k'\ne0$ and test with $v=\mathrm{e}^{ik'\cdot x}$: $\inner{K_bu,v}_{\dot H^1}=\abs{k'}^2\widehat{K_bu}_{k'}$, while
\[
    \int b\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu(ik\hat u_k)\cdot\overline{(ik')}=\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu(k\cdot k')\hat u_k
\]
(convolution formula for $b\in A^0$ and $\nabla u\in L^2$; the series converges absolutely since $\abs{k\cdot k'}\le\abs{k'}(\abs{k'}+\abs{\mu})$ and $\abs{\hat u_k}\le\norm{u}$).
Hence
\[
    \widehat{K_bu}_{k'}=\sum_\mu\hat b_\mu\,\frac{k\cdot k'}{\abs{k'}^2}\,\hat u_k,\qquad k'\ne0.
\]
Coefficientwise, $\abs{k'}^2-\mu\cdot k-\abs{\mu}^2=\abs{k}^2+\mu\cdot k=k\cdot k'$, because $\abs{k'}^2=\abs{k}^2+2\mu\cdot k+\abs{\mu}^2$; dividing by $\abs{k'}^2$ gives the three terms $\Pi M_b$, $R\Gamma(b,\cdot)$ and $-R\mathcal{M}_b$.

The splitting is legitimate because the three series converge absolutely for each $k'$: for $k\ne0$,
\[
    \abs{\mu}^2\abs{\hat u_k}=\frac{\abs{\mu}^2\abs{w_k}}{\abs{k}}\le\abs{\mu}\Bigl(\frac{\abs{k'}}{\abs{k}}+1\Bigr)\abs{w_k}\le\abs{\mu}(\abs{k'}+1)\norm{u}_1,
\]
so $\sum_\mu\abs{\mu}^2\abs{\hat b_\mu}\abs{\hat u_k}\le(\abs{k'}+1)\norm{b}_{A^1}\norm{u}_1$.
Each term lies in $\dot H^1$: for $R\mathcal{M}_b$, Lemma~\ref{lem:bookkeeping} applies with $c=\abs{\mu}^2/\abs{k'}^2$ and $m_\mu(k)=\abs{\mu}^2/(\abs{k'}\abs{k})\le2\abs{\mu}$ by \eqref{eq:F1}, which gives $\norm{R\mathcal{M}_bu}_1\le2\norm{b}_{A^1}\norm{u}_1$; the other two terms are handled in the same way.

\smallskip
\emph{The case $b\in A^2$.}
The remainder has $c(k',\mu)=-(\mu\cdot k+\abs{\mu}^2)/\abs{k'}^2$, and the analogue of \eqref{eq:bookkeeping} with $\abs{k'}^2$ in place of $\abs{k'}$ gives a bound by
\[
    \sum_\mu\abs{\hat b_\mu}\sup_k\frac{\abs{\mu}\abs{k}+\abs{\mu}^2}{\abs{k}}\le\norm{b}_{A^1}+\norm{b}_{A^2},
\]
so the remainder maps $\dot H^1$ into $\dot H^2$.
head: environment

label: rem:R-classical
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:R-classical}
Theorem~\ref{thm:representation} is the classical structure in the form we need and is not claimed as new.
Iterative methods for nonseparable elliptic equations based on fast constant-coefficient solvers go back to Concus and Golub \cite{CG73}; for preconditioning by the inverse Laplacian, the condition number is controlled by the range of the coefficient \cite{NHT09}; the boundedness of $K_b$ on $\dot H^1$ is an instance of the theory of equivalent operators \cite{FMP90}.
In the terminology of Axelsson and Kar\'atson \cite{AK07,AK09} (see also \cite{AK04}), two operators are compact-equivalent if the preconditioned operator is a multiple of the identity plus a compact operator; $L_0$ and $L_a$ are equivalent but not compact-equivalent, since by Theorem~\ref{thm:representation} (for $b\in A^2$) $I+K_b=\bar a^{-1}L_0^{-1}L_a$ is a compact perturbation of the multiplication-type operator $\Pi M_{a/\bar a}$ on $\dot H^1$, not of a multiple of the identity; accordingly, the spectrum of $L_0^{-1}L_a$ contains the range of $a$ \cite{NHT09}, and the eigenvalues of its Galerkin discretisations are localised near the values of $a$ \cite{GMNS19}.
Only the explicit Fourier/$\Gamma$ form of the remainder is specific to this paper.

label: thm:step
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Inexact preconditioned step in operator norm, without Galerkin truncation

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Boundedness and mean zero.}
We have
\[
    \norm{\nabla(bu)}\le\norm{b}_{A^0}\norm{u}_1+\norm{b}_{A^1}\norm{u};
\]
$\Gamma_t(b,\cdot)$ is bounded on $L^2$ with norm at most $\norm{b}_{A^0}/t$;
\[
    \norm{b_\tau}_{A^0}\le\sum_\mu\abs{\hat b_\mu}\min\{\abs{\mu}^2,\tau^{-1}\}\le\tau^{-(1-\theta)/2}\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}};
\]
and $R_m\colon L^2\to\dot H^1$ is bounded by \eqref{eq:HR-consequences}.
Both $I-P_T$ and $R_m$ annihilate constants (their symbols vanish at $0$), so $K^{\mathrm{net}}$ has mean-zero output.
This is needed because $P_tb\,P_tu$ and $u\,b_\tau$ have non-zero mean in general.

\smallskip
\emph{Reduction to trigonometric polynomials.}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:representation}, $\norm{K_b-K_{b'}}\le\norm{b-b'}_{A^0}$, and the bounds just listed are linear in $\norm{b-b'}_{A^{1+\theta}}$; hence $K_b$ and $K^{\mathrm{net}}$ depend continuously on $b$ in $\mathcal{L}(\dot H^1)$ with respect to $\norm{\cdot}_{A^{1+\theta}}$.
The Fourier truncations $b_n$ of $b$ to $\abs{\mu}\le n$ satisfy $b_n\to b$ in $A^{1+\theta}$ and $\norm{b_n}_{A^{1+\theta}}\le\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}$.
It therefore suffices to prove \eqref{eq:Aprime} for trigonometric polynomials $b$, for which $b\in A^2$, $\mathcal{M}_bu=u\,L_0b$, i.e.\ $\mathcal{M}_b=M_{L_0b}$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:representation} gives
\begin{multline*}
    K^{\mathrm{net}}-K_b=\underbrace{(I-P_T-\Pi)M_b}_{(1)}+\underbrace{(R_m-R)\Gamma(b,\cdot)}_{(2)}+\underbrace{R_m(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)}_{(3)}\\
    -\underbrace{(R_m-R)M_{L_0b}}_{(4)}-\underbrace{R_mM_{b_\tau-L_0b}}_{(5)}.
\end{multline*}
Each term has the form \eqref{eq:conv-form}, and we bound $m_\mu(k)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:bookkeeping}; throughout $k'=k+\mu$ and $\abs{k},\abs{k'}\ge1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (1): projection term,} $(I-P_T-\Pi)M_b$.
Here $c=-\mathrm{e}^{-T\abs{k'}^2}$. Since $\abs{k'}\ge1$, $T\ge\frac12$ and $\abs{k}\ge1$,
\begin{gather*}
    m_\mu(k)=\abs{k'}\mathrm{e}^{-T\abs{k'}^2}/\abs{k}\le\mathrm{e}^{-T}.\\
    \text{Contribution}\le\mathrm{e}^{-T}\norm{b}_{A^0}.
\end{gather*}

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (2): inverse error, $\Gamma$ part,} $(R_m-R)\Gamma(b,\cdot)$.
Here $c=(r(\abs{k'}^2)-\abs{k'}^{-2})(-\mu\cdot k)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:HR},
\[
    \abs{c}\le\abs{k'}^{-2}(\delta+2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\abs{k'}>\sqrt\Lambda})\abs{\mu}\abs{k},
\]
so
\begin{gather*}
    m_\mu(k)\le\frac{\abs{\mu}\,(\delta+2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\abs{k'}>\sqrt\Lambda})}{\abs{k'}}\le\abs{\mu}(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2}).\\
    \text{Contribution}\le(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})\norm{b}_{A^1}.
\end{gather*}

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (3): product-defect term,} $R_m(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:product-defect},
\[
    c=r(\abs{k'}^2)(\mu\cdot k)(1-F_t),
    \qquad
    \abs{c}\le(1+\delta)\abs{k'}^{-2}\abs{\mu}\abs{k}\min\{1,2t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)\},
\]
so
\[
    m_\mu(k)\le(1+\delta)\abs{\mu}\,c_t(k,\mu)
    \qquad\text{with}\qquad
    c_t:=\min\{1,2t(\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2)\}/\abs{k'}.
\]

\emph{Case $\abs{k}\ge2\abs{\mu}$.}
Then
\[
    \abs{k'}\ge\abs{k}/2,\qquad\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2\le2\abs{k}^2,
\]
so
\[
    c_t\le2\min\{\abs{k}^{-1},4t\abs{k}\}\le2\sup_{\rho>0}\min\{\rho^{-1},4t\rho\}=4\sqrt t.
\]

\emph{Case $\abs{k}<2\abs{\mu}$.}
Then
\[
    \abs{k'}\ge1,\qquad\abs{k}^2+\abs{\mu}^2<5\abs{\mu}^2,
\]
so
\[
    c_t\le\min\{1,10t\abs{\mu}^2\}\le(10t)^{\theta/2}\abs{\mu}^\theta.
\]

\emph{Both cases.}
\[
    \text{Contribution}\le(1+\delta)\bigl(4\sqrt t\,\norm{b}_{A^1}+(10t)^{\theta/2}\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}\bigr).
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (4): inverse error, $L_0b$ part,} $(R_m-R)M_{L_0b}$.
Here $c=(r(\abs{k'}^2)-\abs{k'}^{-2})\abs{\mu}^2$ and, by \eqref{eq:F1},
\[
    m_\mu(k)\le(\delta+2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\abs{k'}>\sqrt\Lambda})\,g
    \qquad\text{with}\qquad
    g:=\frac{\abs{\mu}^2}{\abs{k'}\abs{k}}\le2\abs{\mu}.
\]

\emph{Band part $\abs{k'}\le\sqrt\Lambda$.}
\[
    m_\mu(k)\le2\delta\abs{\mu}.
\]

\emph{Tail part $\abs{k'}>\sqrt\Lambda$.}
We have
\[
    2g\le2\abs{\mu}/\abs{k'}+2\abs{\mu}/\abs{k},
    \qquad
    2\abs{\mu}/\abs{k'}\le2\abs{\mu}\Lambda^{-1/2}.
\]

\emph{Sub-case $\abs{k}\ge\abs{k'}/2$.}
\[
    2\abs{\mu}/\abs{k}\le4\abs{\mu}\Lambda^{-1/2}.
\]

\emph{Sub-case $\abs{k}<\abs{k'}/2$.}
Then $\abs{\mu}\ge\abs{k'}-\abs{k}>\sqrt\Lambda/2$, so
\[
    \frac{2\abs{\mu}}{\abs{k}}\le2\abs{\mu}=2\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}\abs{\mu}^{-\theta}\le2^{1+\theta}\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}\Lambda^{-\theta/2}\le4\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}\Lambda^{-\theta/2}.
\]

Since $\Lambda^{-1/2}\le\Lambda^{-\theta/2}$ and $\abs{\mu}\le\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}$ for $\abs{\mu}\ge1$ (and $\mu=0$ contributes nothing), the tail is bounded by the larger of the two sub-cases:
\[
    m_\mu(k)\le2\delta\abs{\mu}+6\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}\Lambda^{-\theta/2}\le2\delta\abs{\mu}+10\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}\Lambda^{-\theta/2};
\]
the constants of \eqref{eq:Aprime} are kept because the parameter recipes below are tuned to them.
\[
    \text{Contribution}\le(2\delta+10\Lambda^{-\theta/2})\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (5): channel $b_\tau$,} $R_mM_{b_\tau-L_0b}$.
Here $c=r(\abs{k'}^2)e_\mu$ with
\[
    e_\mu:=\tau^{-1}(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\tau\abs{\mu}^2})-\abs{\mu}^2\in[-\abs{\mu}^2,0].
\]
With $x=\tau\abs{\mu}^2$,
\[
    \abs{e_\mu}=\tau^{-1}\abs{1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}-x}\le x^2/(2\tau),
    \qquad\text{thus}\qquad
    \abs{e_\mu}\le\abs{\mu}^2\min\{1,\tau\abs{\mu}^2/2\}.
\]
Using \eqref{eq:F1} and $\min\{1,x\}\le x^{\theta/2}$,
\begin{gather*}
    m_\mu(k)\le(1+\delta)\,g\,\min\{1,\tau\abs{\mu}^2/2\}\le2(1+\delta)(\tau/2)^{\theta/2}\abs{\mu}^{1+\theta}.\\
    \text{Contribution}\le2(1+\delta)(\tau/2)^{\theta/2}\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}.
\end{gather*}

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Sum.}
Adding (1)--(5) and using $\norm{b}_{A^\sigma}\le\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}$ for $\sigma\le1+\theta$ and $2\Lambda^{-1/2}\le2\Lambda^{-\theta/2}$ gives \eqref{eq:Aprime}.
The argument uses $\Lambda<\infty$ only through the tail terms, which vanish when $\Lambda=\infty$.

\smallskip
\emph{Heat family.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:sinc}, $\delta\le\delta_0\le1/15$, so $1+\delta\le2$, and $T\ge\log75>\frac12$.
In \eqref{eq:Aprime}:
\begin{gather*}
    \mathrm{e}^{-T}=\delta_0/5=\eta_0/(75B);\qquad 3\delta\le\eta_0/(5B);\qquad 12\Lambda^{-\theta/2}=\eta_0/(5B);\\
    2\bigl(4\sqrt t+(10t)^{\theta/2}\bigr)=2\Bigl(\frac4{\sqrt{40}}\Bigl(\frac{\eta_0}{20B}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}+4^{-\theta/2}\frac{\eta_0}{20B}\Bigr)\le2(0.64+1)\frac{\eta_0}{20B}\le\frac{\eta_0}{5B},
\end{gather*}
using $(\eta_0/20B)^{1/\theta}\le\eta_0/(20B)$; and
\[
    4(\tau/2)^{\theta/2}=4\eta_0/(20B)=\eta_0/(5B).
\]
The bracket is at most $\eta_0/B$, and $\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}\le B$.
The count of heat applications follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:sinc} with $\log(\Lambda/\delta_0)=O(\theta^{-1}\log(B/\eta_0))$.

\smallskip
\emph{Mixed family.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:resolvent}, $\delta\le\mathrm{e}^{-T}+1/(1+s)\le\delta_0/2+\delta_0/2=\delta_0$, and $T=\log(30B/\eta_0)>\frac12$.
The bracket in \eqref{eq:Aprime} is at most
\[
    \frac{\delta_0}2+3\delta_0+\frac{\eta_0}{5B}+\frac{\eta_0}{5B}\le\frac{\eta_0}{30B}+\frac{\eta_0}{5B}+\frac{2\eta_0}{5B}\le\frac{\eta_0}{B},
\]
where the $t$- and $\tau$-terms are estimated as in the heat family.

label: rem:sharpness
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:sharpness}
The rate $t^{\theta/2}$ of term (3) cannot in general be improved over the $A^{1+\theta}$ ball.
Take $d=1$ (or one coordinate direction of $\mathbb{T}^d$), $b=2\cos(\mu_0x)$, so that $\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}=2(1+\mu_0)^{1+\theta}$, $u=\mathrm{e}^{ikx}$ with $k=1-\mu_0$, and $t=\mu_0^{-2}$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:product-defect} gives the output of $R(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)$ explicitly; evaluating it yields
\[
    \norm{R(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)}_{\mathcal{L}(\dot H^1)}\ge c\,\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}\,t^{\theta/2}
\]
with $c$ between $0.22$ and $0.29$ for $\theta\in\{1,\frac12,\frac14\}$ and $\mu_0\in\{10,10^2,10^3,10^4\}$ ($c\to(1+\mathrm{e}^{-2})/4\approx0.2838$ as $\mu_0\to\infty$), while the corresponding term of \eqref{eq:Aprime} exceeds this lower bound by a factor between $4.7$ and $15.7$ (between $11$ and $16$ for $\theta=1$).
Hence, for a $b$-independent $t$ of this form, accuracy $\eta_0$ of term (3) uniformly over the ball of radius $B$ requires $t^{\theta/2}\le\eta_0/(cB)$, and the exponent $1/\theta$ in $K_{\mathrm{req}}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:counts}) is structural for this block under the present regularity.
Whether other schemes built from the same primitives need less resolution is open.

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Admissibility.}
Since $\eta_0\le(1-q)/2\le\frac12$, Theorem~\ref{thm:step} applies; moreover $\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}\le B$ and $\norm{b}_\infty\le q$ for $a\in\mathcal{A}_\theta$.

\smallskip
\emph{Mean-zero iterates.}
$v_0=R_mf$ has mean zero because $r(0)=0$, and $K^{\mathrm{net}}$ has mean-zero output by Theorem~\ref{thm:step}; hence all $v_i\in\dot H^1$ and the $\mathcal{L}(\dot H^1)$ bounds apply.

\smallskip
\emph{Error decomposition.}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:reduction} and the recursion,
\[
    G(a,f)=\bar a^{-1}\sum_{j\ge0}(-K_b)^jRf,\qquad N_\varepsilon(a,f)=\bar a^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^N(-K^{\mathrm{net}})^jR_mf.
\]
Put $q':=q+\eta_0\le\frac{1+q}2$, so that $\norm{K^{\mathrm{net}}}\le q'$ and $1-q'\ge(1-q)/2$.
Then
\begin{multline*}
    \bar a\,\norm{G-N_\varepsilon}_1\le\Bigl\|\sum_{j>N}(-K_b)^jRf\Bigr\|_1+\Bigl\|\sum_{j\le N}\bigl[(-K_b)^j-(-K^{\mathrm{net}})^j\bigr]Rf\Bigr\|_1\\
    +\Bigl\|\sum_{j\le N}(-K^{\mathrm{net}})^j(R-R_m)f\Bigr\|_1.
\end{multline*}
The first term is at most $q^{N+1}(1-q)^{-1}\norm{f}$.
For the second, telescoping gives $\norm{K_b^j-(K^{\mathrm{net}})^j}\le j\eta_0q'^{\,j-1}$, so it is at most
\[
    \eta_0(1-q')^{-2}\norm{f}\le4\eta_0(1-q)^{-2}\norm{f}.
\]
For the third, \eqref{eq:HR-consequences} and $\sum_jq'^{\,j}\le(1-q')^{-1}$ give the bound $(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})(1-q')^{-1}\norm{f}$.

\smallskip
\emph{Budget.}
Let $\norm{f}\le1$.
By the choice of $N$, $q^N\le\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)/4$, so the first term is at most $\varepsilon\bar a/4$; for $N=0$ (and $q>0$) the definition of $N$ gives $\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)\ge4$, so $q/(1-q)\le\varepsilon\bar a/4$; for $q=0$ the first term vanishes.

The second term is at most $\varepsilon\bar a/2$ because $\eta_0\le\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)^2/8$.

For the third term, in the heat family $\delta\le\eta_0/(15B)$ and $2\Lambda^{-1/2}=2(\eta_0/60B)^{1/\theta}\le\eta_0/(30B)$; in the mixed family $\delta\le\delta_0=\eta_0/(15B)$ and there is no tail.
In both cases
\[
    \frac{\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2}}{1-q'}\le\frac2{1-q}\cdot\frac{\eta_0}{10B}\le\frac{2\eta_0}{1-q}\le\frac{\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)}4\le\frac{\varepsilon\bar a}4.
\]
The total is at most $\bar a\varepsilon$.

\smallskip
\emph{Dimension.}
No inequality in Lemmas~\ref{lem:bookkeeping}--\ref{lem:reduction} or Theorems~\ref{thm:representation}--\ref{thm:step} involves $d$: the only lattice facts used are $\abs{k}\ge1$ for $k\ne0$ and $\abs{\mu}\le\abs{k}+\abs{k'}$.
If the class is described by $\norm{b}_{H^\sigma}^2:=\sum_\mu(1+\abs{\mu})^{2\sigma}\abs{\hat b_\mu}^2$, then $\norm{b}_{A^{1+\theta}}\le C(d,\sigma)\norm{b}_{H^\sigma}$ for $\sigma>1+\theta+d/2$, with $C(d,\sigma)^2=\sum_{\mu\in\mathbb{Z}^d}(1+\abs{\mu})^{-2(\sigma-1-\theta)}$, and $d$ enters through $B$.

label: prop:counts
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:counts}
Let $N_\varepsilon$ be the scheme of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} in the heat family, and put $L_\varepsilon:=\log(60B/\eta_0)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item \emph{Depth:} $N\le L_\varepsilon/\log(1/q)+1$ ($N=0$ if $q=0$); for $q>0$, $N\sim\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.
    \item \emph{Exponential-sum times:}
    \begin{gather*}
        m\le\Bigl(1+\frac2{\pi^2}L_\varepsilon\Bigr)\Bigl[\Bigl(1+\frac2\theta\Bigr)L_\varepsilon+\log\Bigl(2\log\frac8{h\delta_0}\Bigr)+\log8\Bigr]+1,\\
        \text{i.e. } m\sim\frac2{\pi^2}\Bigl(1+\frac2\theta\Bigr)\log^2\frac1\varepsilon.
    \end{gather*}
    \item \emph{Applications} (Definition~\ref{def:counting}): a block costs $m+3$ heat applications ($2$ at time $t$, $m$ exponential-sum times, $1$ at time $T$), and the precomputation ($P_tb$, $P_\tau b$, $v_0=R_mf$) costs $m+3$; the total is $(N+1)(m+3)=O(\theta^{-1}\log^3(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q))$.
    The number of pointwise products is $3N$.
    \item \emph{Theorem-prescribed reals:} the continuum construction is determined by $2m+4$ reals shared across blocks (the $m$ sinc weights, the $m$ sinc times, and $t,\tau,T,\bar a$), all of them functions of $(\theta,B,a_{\min},a_{\max},\varepsilon)$ through $(h,M,N_{\mathrm{sinc}},T,t,\tau,\bar a)$.
    \item \emph{Magnitudes:} $R_m$ is relatively accurate on the band $\abs{k}\le\sqrt\Lambda=(60B/\eta_0)^{1/\theta}$; the resolution scale of the construction is
    \[
        K_{\mathrm{req}}:=\max\{\sqrt\Lambda,\,t^{-1/2},\,\tau^{-1/2}\}=\max\Bigl\{\Bigl(\frac{60B}{\eta_0}\Bigr)^{1/\theta},\ \sqrt{40}\Bigl(\frac{20B}{\eta_0}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}\Bigr\},
    \]
    where $\tau^{-1/2}=t^{-1/2}/\sqrt{80}$ is never the maximum,
    \[
        \frac{t^{-1/2}}{\sqrt\Lambda}=\sqrt{40}\,3^{-1/\theta}>1
        \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
        \theta>\frac{\log3}{\log\sqrt{40}}\approx0.596,
    \]
    so that $K_{\mathrm{req}}=t^{-1/2}$ for $\theta>0.596$ (in particular for $\theta\in[0.6,1]$) and $K_{\mathrm{req}}=\sqrt\Lambda$ for $\theta<0.596$, and in all cases
    \[
        \Bigl(\frac{60B}{\eta_0}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}\leK_{\mathrm{req}}\le\sqrt{40}\Bigl(\frac{60B}{\eta_0}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}.
    \]
    The smallest heat time is $\mathrm{e}^{-Mh}\in(\delta_0/(8\Lambda),\,\mathrm{e}\,\delta_0/(8\Lambda)]$, so $\mathrm{e}^{-Mh}\asymp\delta_0/\Lambda\asymp(\eta_0/B)^{1+2/\theta}$; the largest multiplier is $1/(2t)=20(20B/\eta_0)^{2/\theta}$.
    With $\eta_0=\varepsilon\bar a(1-q)^2/8$ (the generic case) and $1-q=2/(\kappa+1)$, these quantities are polynomial in $B(\kappa+1)^2/(\varepsilon\bar a)$.
\end{enumerate}
In the mixed family: the depth is $N$; there are $3N+3$ heat applications and $N+1$ resolvent applications; five theorem-prescribed reals; the magnitudes are $s=30B/\eta_0\asymp B(\kappa+1)^2/(\varepsilon\bar a)$ and the same $t,\tau$; and the resolution scale is set by the heat layers, not by $s$:
\[
    K_{\mathrm{req}}=\max\{t^{-1/2},\tau^{-1/2}\}=t^{-1/2}=\sqrt{40}\Bigl(\frac{20B}{\eta_0}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}.
\]
The resolvent satisfies \textup{(H$_R$)}{} with $\Lambda=\infty$ and has no band, but the accuracy of the construction still requires the heat layers to act correctly up to $\abs{k}\asymp t^{-1/2}$.
This coincides with the heat-family $K_{\mathrm{req}}$ for $\theta\ge0.6$ and is smaller only by the constant factor $3^{1/\theta}/\sqrt{40}$ for $\theta<0.596$; both families have $K_{\mathrm{req}}\asymp(B\kappa^2/(\varepsilon\bar a))^{1/\theta}$.

head: environment
name: Density

title: Proof
body_md:
For $u\in V$ let $u_n=(-n\vee u)\wedge n$.
Since truncation is a normal contraction, $u_n\in V$ and $\mathcal{E}(u_n)\le\mathcal{E}(u)$ by the Markov property, and $u_n\to u$ in $L^2$.
Thus $(u_n)$ is bounded in $(V,\mathcal{E}_1)$, every weak limit point equals $u$, and weak lower semicontinuity gives $\mathcal{E}_1(u_n)\to\mathcal{E}_1(u)$; weak convergence and convergence of norms give $u_n\to u$ in $(V,\mathcal{E}_1)$.

label: lem:interpolation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:interpolation}
Let $b\in L^\infty\cap D(L_0)$ with $L_0b\in L^\infty$ and $\sqrt{\Gamma(b)}\in L^\infty$, and let $u\in V_\infty$.
Then, in $L^2$,
\[
    P_t(bu)-P_tb\,P_tu=2\int_0^tP_s\Gamma(P_{t-s}b,P_{t-s}u)\,\mathrm{d} s .
\]
head: environment
name: Interpolation identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\varphi\in L^2\cap L^\infty$, $f_s=P_{t-s}b$, $g_s=P_{t-s}u$ and $A(s)=\int f_sg_s\,P_s\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu$, $s\in[0,t]$.
For $s<t$, $f_s,g_s\in D(L_0)\cap L^\infty$ with $\partial_sf_s=L_0f_s$, $\partial_sg_s=L_0g_s$ in $L^2$, and $L_0f_s=P_{t-s}L_0b$ is bounded; since $f_s,g_s$ are uniformly bounded, $\partial_s(f_sg_s)=(L_0f_s)g_s+f_s(L_0g_s)$ in $L^2$.
With $\psi=P_s\varphi\in V_\infty$ and $\partial_sP_s\varphi=-L_0\psi$,
\[
    A'(s)=\int\bigl[(L_0f_s)g_s+f_s(L_0g_s)\bigr]\psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu-\int f_sg_s\,L_0\psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu .
\]
By (F1), (F2) and the definition of $L_0$,
\begin{align*}
    \int f_sg_sL_0\psi&=\mathcal{E}(\psi,f_sg_s)=\int\bigl[f_s\Gamma(g_s,\psi)+g_s\Gamma(f_s,\psi)\bigr],\\
    \int(L_0f_s)g_s\psi&=\mathcal{E}(f_s,g_s\psi)=\int\bigl[g_s\Gamma(f_s,\psi)+\psi\Gamma(f_s,g_s)\bigr],
\end{align*}
and similarly for the term with $L_0g_s$.
Everything cancels except
\[
    A'(s)=2\int\psi\,\Gamma(f_s,g_s)=2\int\varphi\,P_s\Gamma(f_s,g_s),
\]
by the symmetry of $P_s$ in the form $\int(P_sh)\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int h\,P_s\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ for $h\in L^1$, $\varphi\in L^\infty$ \cite[p.~350]{AGS15}, applied to $h=\Gamma(f_s,g_s)\in L^1$.
$A$ is continuous on $[0,t]$, and $\abs{A'(s)}\le2\mathrm{e}^{K(t-s)}\norm{\sqrt{\Gamma(b)}}_\infty\norm{u}_1\norm{\varphi}$ by (F3), so $A(t)-A(0)=\int_0^tA'$.
Since $A(t)-A(0)=\int[P_t(bu)-P_tb\,P_tu]\varphi$ and $\varphi$ ranges over a dense set, the identity follows.

label: lem:bochner
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bochner}
For $g\in L^\infty$, $r>0$ and $h\in V$,
\[
    \Bigl\|\Gamma\Bigl(\int_0^rP_\sigma g\,\mathrm{d}\sigma,\,h\Bigr)\Bigr\|_{L^2}\le\mathrm{e}^{Kr}\sqrt{2r}\,\norm{g}_\infty\norm{h}_1 .
\]
head: environment
name: Integrated gradient bound

title: Proof
body_md:
The map $\sigma\mapsto P_\sigma g$ is continuous $(0,r]\to V$ with $\norm{P_\sigma g}_1\le(2\mathrm{e}\sigma)^{-1/2}\norm{g}$, so $\int_0^rP_\sigma g\,\mathrm{d}\sigma$ is a Bochner integral in $(V,\mathcal{E}_1)$ and coincides with the $L^2$-integral.
Since $f\mapsto\Gamma(f,h)$ is bounded linear $V\to L^1$,
\[
    \Gamma\Bigl(\int_0^rP_\sigma g\,\mathrm{d}\sigma,h\Bigr)=\int_0^r\Gamma(P_\sigma g,h)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\quad\text{in }L^1.
\]
By (F1) and \eqref{eq:reverse-poincare}, $\norm{\Gamma(P_\sigma g,h)}_{L^2}\le\mathrm{e}^{K\sigma}(2\sigma)^{-1/2}\norm{g}_\infty\norm{h}_1$, which is integrable on $(0,r]$; hence the integral is also an $L^2$-Bochner integral, and $\int_0^r\mathrm{e}^{K\sigma}(2\sigma)^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\le\mathrm{e}^{Kr}\sqrt{2r}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let first $u\in V_\infty$, and put $r=t-s$, $\tilde b_r=P_rb$, $\tilde u_r=P_ru$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:interpolation} and bilinearity,
\[
    (\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,u)=\frac1t\int_0^t\Bigl[(P_s-I)\Gamma(\tilde b_r,\tilde u_r)+\Gamma(\tilde b_r-b,\tilde u_r)+\Gamma(b,\tilde u_r-u)\Bigr]\,\mathrm{d} s=:\frac1t\int_0^tX_s\,\mathrm{d} s,
\]
an $L^2$-Bochner integral (the integrand is continuous in $s\in(0,t)$ and bounded in $L^2$ by (F1), (F3) and Lemma~\ref{lem:bochner}).
Here $\norm{\cdot}_{-1}$ may be taken inside the integral: for $\varphi\in\dot H^1$ with $\norm{\varphi}_1\le1$, pairing the identity with $\varphi$ and using the duality formula for $\norm{\cdot}_{-1}$ gives
\[
    \Bigl|\int\varphi\,(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,u)\,\mathrm{d}\mu\Bigr|\le\frac1t\int_0^t\Bigl|\int\varphi X_s\,\mathrm{d}\mu\Bigr|\,\mathrm{d} s\le\frac1t\int_0^t\norm{X_s}_{-1}\,\mathrm{d} s,
\]
and the supremum over $\varphi$ gives $\norm{(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,u)}_{-1}\le\frac1t\int_0^t\norm{X_s}_{-1}\,\mathrm{d} s$.
Write $\alpha=\norm{\sqrt{\Gamma(b)}}_\infty$ and $\beta=\norm{L_0b}_\infty$.
We estimate the three parts of $X_s$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{(i)}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}, (F1), $\norm{\tilde u_r}_1\le\norm{u}_1$ and (F3) with $P_r\Gamma(b)\le\alpha^2$:
\[
    \norm{(P_s-I)\Gamma(\tilde b_r,\tilde u_r)}_{-1}\le c_0\sqrt s\,\norm{\sqrt{\Gamma(\tilde b_r)}}_\infty\norm{\tilde u_r}_1\le c_0\sqrt s\,\mathrm{e}^{Kr}\alpha\norm{u}_1.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{(ii)}
Since $\tilde b_r-b=-\int_0^rP_\sigma L_0b\,\mathrm{d}\sigma$, Lemma~\ref{lem:bochner} gives
\[
    \norm{\Gamma(\tilde b_r-b,\tilde u_r)}_{-1}\le\norm{\Gamma(\tilde b_r-b,\tilde u_r)}\le\mathrm{e}^{Kr}\sqrt{2r}\,\beta\norm{u}_1.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{(iii)}
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Hminus} and~\ref{lem:spectral}, $\norm{\Gamma(b,\tilde u_r-u)}_{-1}\le(\alpha+\beta)c_0\sqrt r\,\norm{u}_1$.

\smallskip
\noindent
Averaging with $\frac1t\int_0^t\sqrt s\,\mathrm{d} s=\frac1t\int_0^t\sqrt{t-s}\,\mathrm{d} s=\frac23\sqrt t$ and $\mathrm{e}^{Kr}\le\mathrm{e}^{Kt}$,
\[
    \norm{(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,u)}_{-1}\le\sqrt t\,\mathrm{e}^{Kt}\Bigl[\tfrac43c_0\,\alpha+\tfrac23(\sqrt2+c_0)\,\beta\Bigr]\norm{u}_1\le\sqrt t\,\mathrm{e}^{Kt}\bigl[0.851\,\alpha+1.369\,\beta\bigr]\norm{u}_1,
\]
which is at most $1.37\,\mathrm{e}^{Kt}\sqrt t\,\norm{b}_{\mathcal B}\norm{u}_1$.

For $u\in V$, both $\Gamma_t(b,\cdot)$ (with $\norm{\Gamma_t(b,u)}\le\norm{b}_\infty\norm{u}/t$) and $\Gamma(b,\cdot)$ are continuous from $(V,\mathcal{E}_1)$ into $L^2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:density} concludes.

body_md:
Since $P_T1=1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:dirichlet-representation} gives
\begin{multline*}
    K^{\mathrm{net}}-K_b=-P_T\Pi M_b+(R_m-R)\Gamma(b,\cdot)+R_m(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)\\
    -(R_m-R)M_{L_0b}-R_mM_{b_\tau-L_0b}.
\end{multline*}
With $\alpha,\beta$ as above and $u\in\dot H^1$, the five terms are bounded as follows.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (1): projection term,} $P_T\Pi M_b$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}, $\norm{P_T\Pi(bu)}_1\le\mathrm{e}^{-T}\norm{b}_\infty\norm{u}_1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (2): inverse error, $\Gamma$ part,} $(R_m-R)\Gamma(b,\cdot)$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:HR} and (F1), $\norm{(R_m-R)\Gamma(b,u)}_1\le(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})\alpha\norm{u}_1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (3): product-defect term,} $R_m(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,\cdot)$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral} and Theorem~\ref{thm:gamma-consistency},
\[
    \norm{R_m(\Gamma_t-\Gamma)(b,u)}_1\le(1+\delta)\,1.37\,\mathrm{e}^{Kt}\sqrt t\,(\alpha+\beta)\norm{u}_1.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (4): inverse error, $L_0b$ part,} $(R_m-R)M_{L_0b}$.
Here $\norm{(R_m-R)(uL_0b)}_1\le(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})\beta\norm{u}_1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Term (5): channel $b_\tau$,} $R_mM_{b_\tau-L_0b}$.
Write $b_\tau-L_0b=\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau L_0w_\sigma\,\mathrm{d}\sigma$ with $w_\sigma=(P_\sigma-I)b=-\int_0^\sigma P_\rho L_0b\,\mathrm{d}\rho$.
For $u,\varphi\in\dot H^1\cap V_\infty$, (F1), (F2) and the definition of $L_0$ give
\[
    \int(L_0w_\sigma)u\varphi=\int u\,\Gamma(w_\sigma,\varphi)+\int\varphi\,\Gamma(w_\sigma,u),
\]
and Lemma~\ref{lem:bochner} bounds each term by $\mathrm{e}^{K\sigma}\sqrt{2\sigma}\,\beta\norm{u}_1\norm{\varphi}_1$.
Hence
\[
    \norm{uL_0w_\sigma}_{-1}\le2\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{K\sigma}\sqrt\sigma\,\beta\norm{u}_1,
\]
which extends to $u\in\dot H^1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:density}.
Since $\sigma\mapsto L_0w_\sigma=(P_\sigma-I)L_0b$ is continuous into $L^2$ and bounded by $2\beta$ in $L^\infty$, $u(b_\tau-L_0b)=\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau uL_0w_\sigma\,\mathrm{d}\sigma$ is an $L^2$-Bochner integral for $u\in\dot H^1\cap V_\infty$, and the duality argument of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:gamma-consistency} gives
\begin{align*}
    \norm{u(b_\tau-L_0b)}_{-1}&\le\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau\norm{uL_0w_\sigma}_{-1}\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\le\frac1\tau\int_0^\tau2\sqrt2\,\mathrm{e}^{K\sigma}\sqrt\sigma\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\;\beta\norm{u}_1\\
    &\le\tfrac{4\sqrt2}3\,\mathrm{e}^{K\tau}\sqrt\tau\,\beta\norm{u}_1\le1.89\,\mathrm{e}^{K\tau}\sqrt\tau\,\beta\norm{u}_1 ,
\end{align*}
first for $u\in\dot H^1\cap V_\infty$ and then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:density} and the continuity of $u\mapsto u(b_\tau-L_0b)$ from $L^2$ to $L^2$, for all $u\in\dot H^1$. With Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral}, term (5) is at most
\[
    (1+\delta)\,1.89\,\mathrm{e}^{K\tau}\sqrt\tau\,\beta\norm{u}_1.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Sum.}
Terms (2) and (4) combine to $(\delta+2\Lambda^{-1/2})\norm{b}_{\mathcal B}$.
The output has mean zero because $I-P_T$ and $R_m$ annihilate constants, and $K^{\mathrm{net}}$ is bounded on $\dot H^1$ since $\norm{bu}_1\le\norm{b}_\infty\norm{u}_1+\alpha\norm{u}$, $\norm{\Gamma_t(b,\cdot)}_{L^2\to L^2}\le\norm{b}_\infty/t$ and $\norm{b_\tau}_\infty\le\beta$.
